set.statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023 (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, did not detectably change how much people said they drank (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, a step not described as planned); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, all outcomes were self-reported and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those effects cannot be credited to the strategies. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: In 15 trials, mostly with US college students, teaching bundles of safety habits for drinking made very little difference: students drank very slightly less often, but the amount they drank did not clearly change, and no trial tested any one habit on its own. In surveys, students who said they used more safety habits also said they drank less, but most asked about both at the same time, and day by day students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the 2013 review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. So whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
set.population: College students and young adults: 15 randomized trials (2007 to 2023), 13 at US universities, one at a Swedish university and one Australian pilot, mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 (15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed, editors' calculation); and college students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
set.exposure: Protective behavioural strategies taught or prompted in randomized trials, as bundles (limiting or stopping drinking, manner of drinking such as pacing, harm reduction such as a designated driver), alone or within multi-component interventions, mostly brief and digital; and self-reported use of strategies in observational studies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
set.comparator: In trials: assessment only, no intervention, education or other active or attention controls, or the same intervention without a strategies booster; in observational studies: students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional), days without a given strategy (within people, two studies), control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized, and no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
set.outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (quantity, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol), alcohol-related problems and reported strategy use
set.magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).

risk_of_bias.note: Trials (card sc_van_nhat_2026): 14 of 15 at some concerns or high risk of bias by the review's RoB 2 figure, mainly from deviations from the intended interventions and missing outcome data; every outcome self-reported; attrition up to 95%; no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias. Observational studies (card sc_pearson_2013): strategies and outcomes self-reported, nearly always at the same sitting, mostly cross-sectional, unappraised, the review's author a co-author of 7 of the 62 studies.

inconsistency.note: The trial estimates for drinking and problems agree (I² 0% to 22%). The observational findings point different ways by strategy and design (less drinking between people, more on days with some strategies), which the status 'mixed' records; the very heterogeneous effect on reported strategy use (I² 98%) is not a drinking outcome. Not rated down, because the graded finding rests on the trials.

indirectness.note: No trial isolated a single strategy: strategies were taught in bundles, often with personalized normative feedback, against a mix of controls, so the effect of the strategies themselves, or of strategies people choose on their own, is not measured; almost all participants were young US university students.

imprecision.note: The intervals for quantity, frequency and problems are narrow and exclude more than a small effect (none goes beyond −0.19); the problems estimate reaches no difference.

publication_bias.note: No funnel asymmetry in any pool, though with 6 to 9 trials the tests have little power; English-language peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature. Not rated down.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk, self-reported outcomes) and indirectness (bundles taught with other components, not single strategies; US students), giving low for what the trials show: teaching bundles of strategies changed reported drinking very little. The relation stays insufficient evidence for the claim's question, whether the strategies themselves lower drinking or harms: no trial tested any single strategy, the bundles' effects are very small and partly attributable to other components, and the observational associations, which by themselves would be very low (narrative review only), point different ways by design. The meta-analysis is AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional: its list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read), searched English-language peer-reviewed reports only, and its abstract leads with estimates made after dropping a trial; its PRISMA counts do not add up (564 records by database against 514 printed). Counted once: Larimer et al. (2007) and Sugarman and Carey (2009), described in the 2013 review, are among the meta-analysis's trials. Status mixed: the observational findings differ in direction by strategy and design, with only the review author's untested explanation, while the trials show very small or no effects. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review.

statement

In an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, followed for 28 days, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested; it relates test results to what people reported doing next, measures behaviour rather than harm and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect.

In an observational study of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in three US states, followed for 28 days in 2023 (Gelberg et al., 2025, read in full), a fentanyl test-strip result showing fentanyl, compared with one not showing it, went with more reports of using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, and the contrast in the amount people reported using was largest when the drugs tested included illicit benzodiazepines (odds ratio 19.9 for reporting less rather than the same or more, against 2.2 for opioids alone); after a result not showing fentanyl on such drugs, using more was reported in a modelled 66 in 100 cases (37 in 100 for opioids alone). The fold reductions that the paper's abstract, and the review's table, give are these odds ratios, not measured falls in the amount used; the study relates self-reported results to self-reported behaviour, measures neither harm nor overdose and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect.
